opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the parts I find most satisfying, because it's where the replacement model stops being just a nice story and becomes something you can actually check.

The setup is that we train a replacement model, in our case a cross-layer transcoder, that tries to reproduce what the MLPs in the original model are doing, but using sparse, more interpretable features. When we look at an example like the poetry one, where the model has to finish a rhyming couplet, we find a feature that seems to represent the concept "rabbit," and it's active before the model has written the word. It looks like the model is planning ahead: it has picked "rabbit" as the rhyme target and is going to build the line toward it.

But that's a claim about the replacement model. The question is whether the real model is doing the same thing. The bridge is that each feature has a decoder direction. It writes a specific vector into the residual stream of the original model, at specific layers. So the feature isn't just an abstract node in a graph. It corresponds to a concrete direction in the original model's activation space.

To intervene, you take that decoder direction and edit the original model's activations along it. You can subtract it to suppress the feature, or add a scaled version to inject it. Then you let the original model run forward as normal, with its own attention and MLPs, not the replacement, and see what happens to the output.

In the rabbit case, if you turn down the rabbit feature at the end of the first line, the model doesn't fall apart. It picks a different rhyme, like "habit," and writes a coherent line ending there. If you inject a different concept, say "green," it rewrites the line to end on "green," even though that breaks the rhyme. That tells you this direction is actually being used for planning in the real model, and that it shapes how the whole line is built, not just the final word.

There are some caveats. The replacement model isn't perfect. There's reconstruction error, and when you intervene you're stepping a bit outside the distribution the model normally sees, so you have to pick the strength carefully. Too little does nothing, too much breaks things. There's also the question of where to intervene. Features in a cross-layer transcoder write to several layers, so you have to decide whether to patch at one point or across the layers it touches. We usually treat it as a hypothesis test. The attribution graph gives you a prediction, something like "if this feature matters, removing it should change the output in this specific way," and then you check that prediction on the real model. When the prediction holds, as it did with the rabbit example, you have much more confidence that the mechanism is real and not an artifact of the replacement.

r001.rationale: It identifies the feature’s decoder direction as a vector written into the original model’s residual stream at specific layers, and says that direction can be injected into the original model.

r002.rationale: It says subtracting the rabbit direction suppresses the feature, then describes testing this in the original model: turning it down leads to a different rhyme ending, such as “habit,” rather than “rabbit.”

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the things I find most satisfying about the whole approach, because it closes the loop between "we think we see something" and "we actually checked."

So let me back up for a second. The replacement model is this thing we build where we swap out the neurons of the original model, which are really hard to interpret, for a much larger set of features that are sparse and, hopefully, monosemantic. So you get something like a "rabbit" feature, which fires on tokens related to rabbits, and in the poetry example, it fires at the end of a line when the model is planning to rhyme with "grab it" or something like that. And you can trace the circuit in the replacement model and see, okay, this feature is reading from the "grab it" feature and writing into the features that eventually produce "rabbit" at the end of the next line.

But the replacement model is not the real model. It's an approximation. It has some error, and the attribution graphs we draw are a hypothesis about what's going on. So the question is, how do you check?

The key thing is that every feature in the replacement model has a direction in the original model's activation space. When we train these things, the feature is defined as, you know, a linear read from the residual stream, and then it writes back with a decoder vector. So the "rabbit" feature corresponds to a vector, a direction in the actual activations of the real model at a particular layer. That's the bridge.

So the intervention is really simple conceptually. You run the original model, the real Claude, on the prompt. At the layer where that feature lives, you reach into the residual stream and you either subtract that direction, which is suppressing the feature, or you add a multiple of it, which is activating it. And then you just let the real model keep going and see what it does. You're not touching the replacement model at all at that point. You're using it as a map to tell you where to intervene, but the experiment happens in the actual network.

And so in the poetry case, if you suppress the "rabbit" direction after the first line, the model, the real model, now writes a line that ends in something like "habit" instead. It's still rhyming, it's still coherent, it just picked a different plan. And if you inject the "rabbit" direction into a totally different context where it has no business being, the model will go out of its way to end the line with "rabbit." That's the thing that convinces you the feature is doing what the graph said it was doing. If you intervene and nothing happens, or something weird happens, then your hypothesis was wrong, or the replacement model was missing something important.

There are a couple of subtleties. One is you have to pick the magnitude. Subtracting the feature's activation is pretty well defined, but when you're adding, how much do you add? We usually scale it relative to how strongly the feature naturally fires, and you try a range. If you crank it too hard the model just starts saying "rabbit rabbit rabbit" and that's not really telling you anything about the circuit. Another is that you often want to intervene at a specific token position, because the claim is about planning at the end of the line, not about rabbits in general.

And then the other thing I'd say is, the intervention is also how you figure out where the replacement model is wrong. Because sometimes you do the ablation and the downstream effect is much smaller than the graph predicted, and that's telling you there's a parallel pathway through the error terms, through the stuff the replacement model didn't capture. So it's not just a validation step. It's also a way of measuring how much you should trust your own picture.

r001.rationale: It identifies the rabbit feature’s decoder vector as a direction in the original model’s activation space and says to add that direction at the corresponding layer.

r002.rationale: It describes subtracting the rabbit direction in the original model and says the model then ends the line with “habit” instead of “rabbit,” matching the predicted suppression effect.

astra-6.text:
The key is that the replacement model’s features map back into the original model’s activations. So if we find a feature that seems to represent rabbits, we can take the direction associated with that feature and use it to intervene in the original model—adding more of it, for example, at the corresponding layer.

Then we run the original model with that intervention and see how its behavior changes. Does it become more likely to talk about rabbits? If we suppress that feature, does that likelihood decrease? That gives us a causal test. We’re moving from “this feature activates when rabbits come up” to “changing this feature actually changes the model’s behavior in the way we predicted.”

r001.rationale: It describes taking the rabbit feature’s direction from the replacement model and intervening in the original model at the corresponding layer, which conveys the decoder vector’s role as the intervention direction.

r002.rationale: It mentions suppressing the feature and checking whether rabbit-related behavior decreases, but does not describe injecting a negatively scaled decoder vector or testing whether a sentence stops ending in “rabbit.”

sol-6.1.text:
The key is that the replacement model uses the same activation space as the original model. So if a feature in the replacement model corresponds to “rabbit,” we can take the direction that feature writes into the residual stream and use it to intervene in the original model.

For example, we can add that direction at a particular layer and token position, or subtract it to suppress the feature, and then see how the model’s predictions change. If we think that feature helps produce an answer about rabbits, does suppressing it reduce the probability of that answer? Does adding it push the model toward rabbit-related answers?

That gives us a causal test. The label “rabbit” is our interpretation of the feature; the intervention tests whether it actually plays the role we think it does.

r001.rationale: It identifies the feature’s residual-stream direction and says to add that direction to the original model at a layer, conveying the decoder-vector intervention.

r002.rationale: It describes subtracting the direction to suppress the feature, but does not specify a negatively scaled decoder vector or test whether that prevents a sentence from ending in “rabbit.”
